html:
Mars clock vs MEDASolar zenith angle error 0.001 ± 0.086° (95 % within 0.20°) over 5616 samples on 117 sols; LTST within 5 s.
Elevation vs roverDEM minus rover-localised geoid height: 0.2 ± 0.4 m (480 points); HiRISE-covered 0.2 ± 0.4 m. Caveat: JPL localises the rover against these same orbital maps, so this confirms our warping and datum handling, not independent DEM accuracy.
Slope vs rover tiltRover chassis tilt median 4.5°; our walking-scale slope (90th pct) is at or above the measured tilt at 74 % of 480 points (r = 0.72).
False no-go rateRobotic-scout vetoes forbid 2 % of 703 real Perseverance positions (all cliff-edge stand-offs; keep-out zones excluded because they mark where the rover itself was). Suited-walk limits forbid 2 %.
Route reproductionOn 30 real drives where Perseverance went around something (path at least 1.15x the straight line, 0.4-2 km), our robotic-scout route stays on average 38 m from the rover's actual path vs 34 m for a straight line (closer in 14 of 30); 75 % of planned points lie within 50 m of the real drive (straight 76 %). On 15 direct drives the figures are 19 and 15 m. Result: route geometry does NOT reproduce JPL's drives better than a straight line. Rover drives are shaped by science stops, AutoNav and sub-metre hazards, and the public waypoint record is sparse (one point per drive end), so geometric match is a weak test.
Hazard model vs JPL's choicesOn the 30 detour drives, mean hazard index along the rover's real path is 0.182 vs 0.208 along the straight line (real path lower on 21 of 30); our risk-aware route scores 0.111.
Bedform avoidanceCells with strong bedform evidence: 3 % on the rover's path vs 7 % of the surrounding 1 km corridor.
WeightsAHP consistency ratios: L1 0.009, safety (foot) 0.000, safety (rover) 0.008, terrain 0.004 (all < 0.10). Perturbing every top-level judgement at random (log-sd 0.4, 40 runs) keeps 100 % of the balanced route within 30 m of nominal on average (worst run 99 %; 100 % of runs keep at least 80 %); EVA time 3.88-3.97 h (nominal 3.94 h).

What this shows: the clock, terrain registration and slope layer agree with real rover data, and the hazard layer ranks the paths JPL actually chose as safer than the straight line. What it does not show: that our routes match where a rover team would drive, or that suited-crew limits are right (no human has walked on Mars). Computed by validation/validate.mjs on 2026-10-25 with the shipped engine and real data.
